title: Agentic AI & Hyperautomation

meta_description: Agentic AI & Hyperautomation delivered as workforce design: seven practices on one execution spine — mined candidates, policy-bounded agents, replayable evidence. Six gates, twelve sector playbooks, one fleet console.

blocks.x: Hyperautomation succeeds as workforce design, not as tool rollout. Agentic AI & Hyperautomation runs seven practices that mine the work, prove the ROI before the build, deploy role-scoped agents under policy bounds, and manage the resulting digital workforce with the same discipline — capacity, shifts, versioning, retirement — you apply to people.

The buyers who arrive here carry one of two documents: a process inventory nobody defends, or an automation backlog full of bots whose business case expired after the pilot. Both are symptoms of the same missing discipline — automation decisions made without mined evidence, priced economics and a checkpoint design. The seven practices in this domain exist to install that discipline before the next license renewal, not after.

Seven practices carry the domain, from process mining through document intelligence to digital-workforce orchestration. They share one substrate — the policy engine, the replay store and the ROI ledger — and every practice contributes to and is constrained by it. That is what makes the practices composable: a document pipeline built by one practice replays under the same evidence store that audits an agent fleet built by another.

blocks.x: Where automation programs stall — and the operating discipline that prevents it
blocks.sub: Failure economics from delivery, distilled into four structural controls

blocks.x: The stall pattern is predictable enough to name: licenses bought on a vendor's workshop, bots deployed against processes that were never mined, a coverage number nobody owns, and an exception backlog that quietly becomes the old process with extra steps. Spend compounds while the audited benefit stays flat — the economics die in exactly that sequence. The operating discipline here reverses it: mined evidence before funding, priced economics before build, checkpoint design before autonomy, and a coverage metric with a named owner from the first week.

The governance argument is what wins the board: every agent action replays, checkpoints sit where the risk matrix says they must, and autonomy is earned by evidence rather than configured by enthusiasm. That discipline is the difference between a program the auditors sign off and one they suspend.

blocks.x: Authority is the design problem
blocks.sub: Why tool grants, checkpoint placement and kill decisions are engineered as first-class structures

blocks.x: Automation programs fail at the joints, and the joints are between practices, not inside them. A mined candidate list that nobody prices dies in procurement; an agent fleet without a policy spine dies at the first access review; a policy spine without a replay store dies at the first internal audit. The domain is therefore engineered as one execution spine: mining prices the work, design places the checkpoints, the fleet executes under policy, and the evidence store makes every claim reconstructable. Each practice can be bought separately — the spine cannot, which is why the reference architecture holds all four layers even for a single-practice engagement.

The technical debate we settle with every client is where authority sits. Tool grants belong to role definitions, not to agent builders; checkpoint placement belongs to a signed risk matrix, not to developer convenience; the kill decision on a candidate belongs to the ROI ledger, not to stakeholder enthusiasm. Programs that leave these three calls informal produce impressive demos and indefensible operations. The gates in this domain encode exactly those calls — evidence, not narrative, moves a candidate from mining to design to production.

items: One spine, four practices
Mining, design, fleet and evidence share identifiers, schemas and gates — no orphan artifacts.
Authority is explicit
Tool grants from roles, checkpoints from risk matrix, kill decisions from the ROI ledger.
Replay is the contract
Any action, any day, reconstructable from the trace within one business day.
Gates bind, not advise
A candidate without priced economics does not advance; a cohort without evidence does not go live.
We already run RPA — does this domain replace it?

No. The mining practice prices what should stay as RPA, what becomes an agent with tool grants, and what should never be automated; the integration practice then brings both under one policy and replay spine, so the estate is governed as one fleet instead of two stacks.
How do you stop an agent from doing damage?

Three layers: deny-by-default tool grants issued to role definitions, checkpoints placed by the signed risk matrix, and a policy engine that can halt any action class in one place. Every action replays, so containment is a reading exercise, not an investigation.
What does the two-week diagnostic actually produce?

A ranked candidate list mined from your event logs with owners and kill reasons, a scored gate map, and a checkpoint design for the first process family — signed by your side, and usable by whoever builds next.
Who owns the automation after you leave?
The coverage metric has a named owner from week one; the fleet runs under your operations team with the runbook, the console and the quarterly re-baseline cadence the industrialize phase installs.
Can we start with just document processing?

Yes — intelligent document processing is a common entry practice. The spine still applies: the documents it reads are versioned sources, its outputs land in systems of record through the integration practice, and its decisions replay into the same evidence store.

blocks.x: Bring the process your CFO calls expensive and your auditors call fragile — the two-week diagnostic will rank what should be automated, what should not, and what the checkpoint design would look like.
